claim: A growing yeast cell imports approximately 14 million ribosomal proteins into the nucleus for ribosome production within a single generation time.
source: Within a single generation time a growing yeast cell imports ∼14 million ribosomal proteins (r-proteins) into the nucleus for ribosome production.
evidence: This is stated in the abstract as a quantitative assertion about r-protein import.

claim: Tsr2 is a conserved nuclear carrier that coordinates transfer of the r-protein eS26 to the earliest assembling pre-ribosome, the 90S.
source: Here, we report the discovery of a conserved nuclear carrier Tsr2 that coordinates transfer of the r-protein eS26 to the earliest assembling pre-ribosome, the 90S.
evidence: This is the main finding reported in the abstract.

claim: Tsr2 efficiently dissociates importin:eS26 complexes via an atypical RanGTP-independent mechanism.
source: In vitro studies revealed that Tsr2 efficiently dissociates importin:eS26 complexes via an atypical RanGTP-independent mechanism that terminates the import process.
evidence: This is supported by in vitro dissociation assays shown in the manuscript.

claim: Tsr2 binds the released eS26 and shields it from proteolysis.
source: Subsequently, Tsr2 binds the released eS26, shields it from proteolysis, and ensures its safe delivery to the 90S pre-ribosome.
evidence: This is supported by proteolysis protection experiments and aggregation assays.

claim: The budding yeast ribosome consists of a large 60S subunit containing three different rRNAs (25S, 5.8S, 5S) and 46 ribosomal proteins.
source: In the eukaryotic model organism budding yeast, this universal translating machine is built of two subunits: a large subunit (60S) consisting of three different rRNAs (25S, 5.8S, 5S) and 46 ribosomal proteins (r-proteins) and a small subunit (40S) that contains a single rRNA (18S) and 33 r-proteins (Ben-Shem et al., 2011; Klinge et al., 2011; Rabl et al., 2011).
evidence: This is supported by citations to structural studies.

claim: The budding yeast ribosome consists of a small 40S subunit containing a single rRNA (18S) and 33 ribosomal proteins.
source: In the eukaryotic model organism budding yeast, this universal translating machine is built of two subunits: a large subunit (60S) consisting of three different rRNAs (25S, 5.8S, 5S) and 46 ribosomal proteins (r-proteins) and a small subunit (40S) that contains a single rRNA (18S) and 33 r-proteins (Ben-Shem et al., 2011; Klinge et al., 2011; Rabl et al., 2011).
evidence: This is supported by citations to structural studies.

claim: Eukaryotic ribosome assembly takes place in three distinct cellular territories: the nucleolus, the nucleoplasm and the cytoplasm.
source: Assembly of the eukaryotic ribosome takes place in three distinct cellular territories: the nucleolus, the nucleoplasm and the cytoplasm (Woolford and Baserga, 2013; Gerhardy et al., 2014).
evidence: This is supported by citations to review articles.

claim: RNA polymerase I drives production of the 35S pre-rRNA transcript in the nucleolus, which initiates the assembly process.
source: RNA polymerase I drives production of the 35S pre-rRNA transcript in the nucleolus, which initiates the assembly process.
evidence: This is established knowledge about ribosome biogenesis.

claim: The 35S pre-rRNA transcript undergoes co-transcriptional modification and processing.
source: The emerging 35S pre-rRNA transcript undergoes co-transcriptional modification and processing (Osheim et al., 2004; Kos and Tollervey, 2010), and associates primarily with 40S subunit r-proteins and ∼50 assembly factors to form the earliest pre-ribosome, the 90S (Dragon et al., 2002; Grandi et al., 2002; Schäfer et al., 2003).
evidence: This is supported by citations to studies on pre-rRNA processing.

claim: The 35S pre-rRNA associates primarily with 40S subunit r-proteins and approximately 50 assembly factors to form the earliest pre-ribosome, the 90S.
source: The emerging 35S pre-rRNA transcript undergoes co-transcriptional modification and processing (Osheim et al., 2004; Kos and Tollervey, 2010), and associates primarily with 40S subunit r-proteins and ∼50 assembly factors to form the earliest pre-ribosome, the 90S (Dragon et al., 2002; Grandi et al., 2002; Schäfer et al., 2003).
evidence: This is supported by citations to proteomic studies of the 90S particle.

claim: Nuclear maturation of pre-ribosomal particles requires the release of assembly factors, a process thought to require more than 50 energy consuming enzymes.
source: Nuclear maturation of pre-ribosomal particles also requires the release of assembly factors, a process thought to require >50 energy consuming enzymes (Strunk and Karbstein, 2009; Kressler et al., 2010).
evidence: This is supported by citations to review articles on ribosome assembly.

claim: In yeast, export factors include the exportin Xpo1, which recognizes nuclear export sequences (NESs) in a RanGTP-dependent manner.
source: In yeast, export factors include the exportin Xpo1, which recognizes nuclear export sequences (NESs) in a RanGTP-dependent manner, and additional factors (Tschochner and Hurt, 2003).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to a review article.

claim: Immature 20S pre-rRNA is endonucleolytically cleaved into mature 18S rRNA by the nuclease Nob1.
source: Within the pre-40S particle, immature 20S pre-rRNA is endonucleolytically cleaved into mature 18S rRNA by the nuclease Nob1 rendering the subunit translation competent (Fatica et al., 2004; Lamanna and Karbstein, 2009; Pertschy et al., 2009).
evidence: This is supported by citations to studies on Nob1 function.

claim: Multiple conserved ATPases (Prp43, Rio2, Rli1 and Fap7), the Prp43-activator Pfa1, the kinase Rio1, the assembly factor Ltv1 and the r-protein uS11 are implicated in 20S pre-rRNA cleavage.
source: Additionally, multiple conserved ATPases Prp43, Rio2, Rli1 and Fap7, the Prp43-activator Pfa1, the kinase Rio1, the assembly factor Ltv1 and the r-protein uS11 (yeast Rps14) are implicated in this cleavage step (Geerlings et al., 2003; Vanrobays et al., 2003; Jakovljevic et al., 2004; Granneman et al., 2005; Pertschy et al., 2009; Strunk et al., 2012; Hellmich et al., 2013).
evidence: This is supported by citations to multiple studies.

claim: Ribosome assembly accounts for the major proportion of nucleocytoplasmic transport in a growing yeast cell.
source: In addition to the tremendous energy required to assemble ribosomes, this process also accounts for the major proportion of the nucleocytoplasmic transport in a growing yeast cell (Rout et al., 1997; Sydorskyy et al., 2003).
evidence: This is supported by citations to studies on nucleocytoplasmic transport.

claim: In yeast, the importin Kap123 is an important mediator of r-protein import.
source: In yeast, the importin Kap123 has been shown to be an important mediator of r-protein import, but the related importin Pse1 can functionally substitute Kap123 in vivo (Rout et al., 1997; Schlenstedt et al., 1997).
evidence: This is supported by citations to studies on r-protein import.

claim: The related importin Pse1 can functionally substitute Kap123 in vivo.
source: In yeast, the importin Kap123 has been shown to be an important mediator of r-protein import, but the related importin Pse1 can functionally substitute Kap123 in vivo (Rout et al., 1997; Schlenstedt et al., 1997).
evidence: This is supported by citations to studies on r-protein import.

claim: R-proteins contain large unstructured regions that form intricate interactions with rRNA within the mature ribosome and are prone to non-specific interactions with nucleic acids, aggregation and proteolytic degradation in their non-assembled state.
source: Unlike other cargos, r-proteins contain large unstructured regions that form intricate interactions with rRNA within the mature ribosome and are prone to non-specific interactions with nucleic acids, aggregation and proteolytic degradation in their non-assembled state (Jäkel and Görlich, 1998; Jäkel et al., 2002; Klinge et al., 2011; Rabl et al., 2011).
evidence: This is supported by citations to structural and biochemical studies.

claim: Importins have been implicated to chaperone basic r-proteins during their transport to the nucleus.
source: In addition to their transport role, importins have been implicated to chaperone basic r-proteins during their transport to the nucleus (Jäkel et al., 2002).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to a study on importin function.

claim: Previous genome-wide studies revealed a strong accumulation of immature 20S pre-rRNA in a TSR2 deficient yeast strain (tsr2Δ).
source: Previous genome-wide studies revealed a strong accumulation of immature 20S pre-rRNA in a TSR2 (20 S rRNA accumulation 2) deficient yeast strain (tsr2Δ) (Peng et al., 2003).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to a previous study.

claim: Tsr2 is a conserved 23.7 kDa protein.
source: Tsr2 is a conserved 23.7 kDa protein (Figure 1—figure supplement 1A) with no identified structural homologues that could provide clues into its role in 20S pre-rRNA processing.
evidence: This is stated in the text and supported by a sequence alignment figure.

claim: Tsr2 has no identified structural homologues.
source: Tsr2 is a conserved 23.7 kDa protein (Figure 1—figure supplement 1A) with no identified structural homologues that could provide clues into its role in 20S pre-rRNA processing.
evidence: This is stated in the text.

claim: On repressive glucose media, Tsr2 protein levels were undetectable in the PGAL1-TSR2 strain.
source: On repressive glucose media, Tsr2 protein levels were undetectable and the PGAL1-TSR2 strain was severely impaired in growth compared to a wild-type (WT) strain between 20–37°C (Figure 1A).
evidence: This is shown in Figure 1A by Western blot analysis.

claim: The PGAL1-TSR2 strain was severely impaired in growth compared to a wild-type strain between 20–37°C on repressive glucose media.
source: On repressive glucose media, Tsr2 protein levels were undetectable and the PGAL1-TSR2 strain was severely impaired in growth compared to a wild-type (WT) strain between 20–37°C (Figure 1A).
evidence: This is shown in Figure 1A by growth assays.

claim: Tsr2-TAP, Tsr2-GFP and Tsr2-3xGFP fusion proteins predominantly localize to the nucleus.
source: These cell-biological studies revealed that both fusion proteins predominantly localize to the nucleus (Figure 1B).
evidence: This is shown in Figure 1B by microscopy.

claim: Strains expressing Tsr2-TAP, Tsr2-GFP, and Tsr2-3xGFP fusion proteins were not impaired in growth.
source: The strains expressing the various fusion proteins were not impaired in growth (Figure 1A) suggesting that addition of the -GFP, -TAP, and -3xGFP tags did not affect Tsr2 function.
evidence: This is shown in Figure 1A by growth assays.

claim: PGAL1-TSR2 cells grown on glucose showed cytoplasmic uS5-GFP localization, indicating no apparent impairment in nuclear export of pre-40S subunits.
source: Surprisingly, PGAL1-TSR2 cells grown on glucose also showed cytoplasmic uS5-GFP localization (Figure 1—figure supplement 1B), indicating no apparent impairment in nuclear export of pre-40S subunits.
evidence: This is shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1B by microscopy.

claim: Tsr2-depleted cells exhibited strong cytoplasmic accumulation of Cy3-ITS1, indicating that cytoplasmic processing is impaired in these cells.
source: Tsr2-depleted cells exhibited strong cytoplasmic accumulation of Cy3-ITS1 (Figure 1C), indicating that cytoplasmic processing is impaired in these cells.
evidence: This is shown in Figure 1C by FISH analysis.

claim: The polysome profile of Tsr2-depleted cell extracts revealed strongly reduced levels of free 40S subunits and polysomes.
source: In agreement with a role in the 40S biogenesis pathway, the polysome profile of Tsr2-depleted cell extracts revealed strongly reduced levels of free 40S subunits and polysomes (Figure 1D, top panel).
evidence: This is shown in Figure 1D by polysome profiling.

claim: Northern analyses revealed that mature 25S rRNA and immature 20S pre-rRNA co-peak in Tsr2-depleted cells, indicating accumulation of 80S-like particles.
source: Northern analyses revealed that mature 25S rRNA and immature 20S pre-rRNA co-peak (Figure 1D, bottom panel), indicating accumulation of 80S-like particles, similar to the one seen upon Fap7-depletion (Granneman et al., 2005; Strunk et al., 2012).
evidence: This is shown in Figure 1D by Northern blot analysis.

claim: Tsr2 did not co-sediment with the 40S peak or with heavier fractions, but was found exclusively in lighter fractions at the top of the gradient.
source: Unexpectedly, Tsr2 did not co-sediment with the 40S peak or with heavier fractions, but was found exclusively in lighter fractions at the top of the gradient (Figure 1E).
evidence: This is shown in Figure 1E by sucrose gradient fractionation and Western blot.

claim: Tsr2-TAP co-enriched stoichiometric amounts of the eukaryotic specific r-protein eS26.
source: In agreement with the sedimentation studies above, Tsr2-TAP did not isolate a pre-40S particle. Instead, Tsr2-TAP co-enriched stoichiometric amounts of the eukaryotic specific r-protein eS26 (Figure 1F; Peng et al., 2003).
evidence: This is shown in Figure 1F by tandem affinity purification and mass spectrometry.

claim: Yeast two-hybrid analysis revealed a strong interaction between Tsr2 and eS26.
source: Further, yeast two-hybrid analysis revealed a strong interaction between Tsr2 and eS26, as determined by growth on stringent adenine deficient media (Figure 1G).
evidence: This is shown in Figure 1G by yeast two-hybrid assay.

claim: In vitro binding studies using recombinant proteins showed that eS26 and Tsr2 formed a robust complex.
source: In vitro binding studies using recombinant proteins showed that eS26 and Tsr2 formed a robust complex (Figure 1H).
evidence: This is shown in Figure 1H by in vitro binding assay.

claim: In budding yeast, two non-essential genes, RPS26A and RPS26B, encode the r-protein eS26.
source: In budding yeast, two non-essential genes, RPS26A and RPS26B, encode the r-protein eS26.
evidence: This is stated in the text.

claim: The PGAL1-RPS26Arps26bΔ strain did not grow on repressive glucose containing medium.
source: Consistent with an essential function of eS26 in yeast, the PGAL1-RPS26Arps26bΔ strain did not grow on repressive glucose containing medium (Figure 2A).
evidence: This is shown in Figure 2A by growth assay.

claim: eS26-depletion did not induce nuclear accumulation of uS5-GFP, indicating no apparent impairment in pre-40S subunit nuclear export.
source: eS26-depletion did not induce nuclear accumulation of uS5-GFP (Figure 1—figure supplement 1B), indicating no apparent impairment in pre-40S subunit nuclear export.
evidence: This is shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1B by microscopy.

claim: eS26-depleted cells showed a strong cytoplasmic accumulation of Cy3-ITS1, indicating impairment in final 20S pre-rRNA processing.
source: However, these cells showed a strong cytoplasmic accumulation of Cy3-ITS1 (Figure 2B), indicating impairment in final 20S pre-rRNA processing.
evidence: This is shown in Figure 2B by FISH analysis.

claim: Polysome analyses of eS26-depleted cell extracts revealed strongly reduced levels of free 40S subunits.
source: Further, polysome analyses of eS26-depleted cell extracts revealed strongly reduced levels of free 40S subunits (Figure 2C, top panel).
evidence: This is shown in Figure 2C by polysome profiling.

claim: Northern analyses revealed that mature 25S rRNA and immature 20S pre-rRNA co-peaked in eS26-depleted cells, indicating an accumulation of 80S-like particles.
source: Northern analyses revealed that mature 25S rRNA and immature 20S pre-rRNA co-peaked (Figure 2C, bottom panel), indicating an accumulation of 80S-like particles.
evidence: This is shown in Figure 2C by Northern blot analysis.

claim: Both Western and SRM analyses revealed that eS26 co-enriches efficiently with the earliest ribosomal precursor, the 90S, and different pre-ribosomes along the 40S maturation pathway.
source: Both Western and SRM analyses revealed that eS26 co-enriches efficiently with the earliest ribosomal precursor, the 90S, and different pre-ribosomes along the 40S maturation pathway (Figure 3A,B).
evidence: This is shown in Figure 3A and 3B by Western blot and SRM-MS analysis.

claim: In yrb2Δ cells, eS26-GFP accumulated in the nucleus.
source: In contrast, in yrb2Δ cells eS26-GFP accumulated in the nucleus (Figure 3C, right panel).
evidence: This is shown in Figure 3C by microscopy.

claim: Tsr2 did not detectably co-enrich with affinity purified pre-ribosomal particles in the 40S maturation pathway.
source: Consistent with the sedimentation studies and direct binding to only eS26 (Figure 1), Tsr2 did not detectably co-enrich with affinity purified pre-ribosomal particles in the 40S maturation pathway (Figure 3A).
evidence: This is shown in Figure 3A by Western blot analysis of TAP purifications.

claim: The importins Kap123, Kap104 and Pse1 efficiently bound eS26 in vitro.
source: These studies revealed that the importins Kap123, Kap104 and Pse1 efficiently bound eS26 (Figure 4A).
evidence: This is shown in Figure 4A by in vitro binding assay.

claim: None of the importins bound to either Tsr2 or the Tsr2:eS26 complex.
source: In contrast, none of the importins bound to either Tsr2 or the Tsr2:eS26 complex (Figure 4A, Figure 4—figure supplement 1), indicating that eS26 alone specifically interacts with importins.
evidence: This is shown in Figure 4A and Figure 4—figure supplement 1 by in vitro binding assays.

claim: Nuclear uptake of GFP-eS26 was reduced in kap123Δ and kap104Δ cells.
source: Consistent with in vitro binding assays, nuclear uptake of GFP-eS26 was reduced in kap123Δ and kap104Δ cells (Figure 4B), indicating that eS26 import requires these importins.
evidence: This is shown in Figure 4B by microscopy.

claim: Tsr2-3xGFP mislocalizes to the cytoplasm in the kap123Δ mutant.
source: We found that Tsr2-3xGFP mislocalizes to the cytoplasm in the kap123Δ mutant, but not in other importin mutants for e.g. kap104Δ and pse1-1 (Figure 4C).
evidence: This is shown in Figure 4C by microscopy.

claim: RanGTP was able to dissociate the Kap104:eS26 complex.
source: Although RanGTP was able to dissociate the Kap104:eS26 complex, and partially dissociate the Pse1:eS26 complex, we did not observe dissociation of the Kap123:eS26 complex even after 1 hr incubation (Figure 4D).
evidence: This is shown in Figure 4D by in vitro dissociation assay.

claim: RanGTP partially dissociated the Pse1:eS26 complex.
source: Although RanGTP was able to dissociate the Kap104:eS26 complex, and partially dissociate the Pse1:eS26 complex, we did not observe dissociation of the Kap123:eS26 complex even after 1 hr incubation (Figure 4D).
evidence: This is shown in Figure 4D by in vitro dissociation assay.

claim: RanGTP did not dissociate the Kap123:eS26 complex even after 1 hr incubation.
source: Although RanGTP was able to dissociate the Kap104:eS26 complex, and partially dissociate the Pse1:eS26 complex, we did not observe dissociation of the Kap123:eS26 complex even after 1 hr incubation (Figure 4D).
evidence: This is shown in Figure 4D by in vitro dissociation assay.

claim: Tsr2 alone efficiently removed eS26 from Kap123, Pse1 and Kap104.
source: Surprisingly, Tsr2 alone efficiently removed eS26 from Kap123, Pse1 and Kap104 (Figure 4—figure supplement 3B,C and data not shown).
evidence: This is shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 3B,C by in vitro dissociation assays.

claim: Tsr2 completely removed eS26 from importins within 1 min incubation.
source: In contrast, Tsr2 completely removed eS26 from these importins within 1 min incubation (Figure 4E, right panel and Figure 4—figure supplement 3E, right panel).
evidence: This is shown in Figure 4E and Figure 4—figure supplement 3E by kinetic dissociation assays.

claim: Tsr2 stably associated with the released eS26.
source: Moreover, Tsr2 stably associated with the released eS26 (Figure 4F, Figure 4—figure supplement 3C).
evidence: This is shown in Figure 4F and Figure 4—figure supplement 3C by in vitro binding assays.

claim: eS26 does not efficiently co-enrich with Enp1-TAP in Tsr2-depleted cells.
source: Consistent with a role for Tsr2 in supplying eS26 to the 90S pre-ribosome, we found that eS26 does not efficiently co-enrich with Enp1-TAP in Tsr2-depleted cells (Figure 5A).
evidence: This is shown in Figure 5A by TAP purification and Western blot.

claim: Western analyses of whole cell extracts derived from Tsr2-depleted cells revealed strongly reduced eS26 protein levels.
source: This lack of enrichment was due to decreased eS26 protein levels, since Western analyses of whole cell extracts derived from Tsr2-depleted cells revealed strongly reduced eS26 protein levels (Figure 5B).
evidence: This is shown in Figure 5B by Western blot analysis.

claim: eS26 protein levels decreased over time upon Tsr2-depletion.
source: These analyses revealed that eS26 protein levels decreased over time upon Tsr2-depletion (Figure 5C).
evidence: This is shown in Figure 5C by time-course Western blot analysis.

claim: Removal of the GST tag from GST-eS26 by PreScission protease resulted in immediate aggregation of free eS26.
source: However, removal of the GST tag after cleavage by PreScission protease resulted in immediate aggregation of free eS26, as determined by a massive increase in the light scattering intensity (Figure 5D).
evidence: This is shown in Figure 5D by aggregation assay.

claim: Tsr2 suppressed the aggregation of recombinant eS26.
source: A concomitant decrease in the light scattering of the reaction mixture was observed (Figure 5D), as the Tsr2 concentration in the cleavage buffer was increased, indicating aggregation of free eS26 was suppressed.
evidence: This is shown in Figure 5D by aggregation assay.

claim: Several mutations in r-proteins have been linked to Diamond-Blackfan anemia (DBA).
source: Mutations in r-proteins have been linked to Diamond-Blackfan anemia (DBA), a rare congenital red blood cell aplasia (Ellis and Lipton, 2008; Ganapathi and Shimamura, 2008; Narla and Ebert, 2010; Ellis and Gleizes, 2011; McCann and Baserga, 2013; Ellis, 2014).
evidence: This is supported by citations to review articles on DBA.

claim: Several mutations in the start codon of RPS26, including two mutations within eS26, D33N and C77W have been linked to DBA.
source: Several mutations in the start codon of RPS26, including two mutations within eS26, D33N and C77W have been linked to DBA (Doherty et al., 2010; Cmejla et al., 2011).
evidence: This is supported by citations to studies on DBA mutations.

claim: The C77W mutation is additionally linked to Klippel-Feil syndrome (KFS), a skeletal developmental disorder in DBA patients.
source: The C77W mutation is additionally linked to Klippel-Feil syndrome (KFS), a skeletal developmental disorder in DBA patients (Cmejla et al., 2011).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to a study on KFS.

claim: The D33N mutant partially rescued the lethality of the eS26-conditional mutant.
source: Whereas the D33N mutant partially rescued the lethality of the eS26-conditional mutant, the C77W variant did not allow any growth (Figure 6A).
evidence: This is shown in Figure 6A by growth assay.

claim: The C77W variant did not allow any growth in the eS26-conditional mutant.
source: Whereas the D33N mutant partially rescued the lethality of the eS26-conditional mutant, the C77W variant did not allow any growth (Figure 6A).
evidence: This is shown in Figure 6A by growth assay.

claim: Both DBA variants (eS26D33N and eS26C77W) resulted in strongly reduced eS26 protein levels.
source: Further, as in the PGAL1-TSR2 strain under repressive conditions, both variants resulted in strongly reduced eS26 protein levels (Figure 6B).
evidence: This is shown in Figure 6B by Western blot analysis.

claim: Both DBA mutants (eS26D33N and eS26C77W) accumulate 20S pre-rRNA in the cytoplasm.
source: Similar to the Tsr2-depletion, both DBA mutants (eS26D33N and eS26C77W) accumulate 20S pre-rRNA in the cytoplasm (Figure 6C).
evidence: This is shown in Figure 6C by FISH analysis.

claim: Both mutant proteins (eS26D33N and eS26C77W) efficiently bound Tsr2.
source: Pull-down assays demonstrated that both mutant proteins efficiently bound Tsr2 (Figure 6D), suggesting these mutations do not contribute to the Tsr2:eS26 interaction surface.
evidence: This is shown in Figure 6D by in vitro binding assay.

claim: The eS26D33N mutant efficiently binds to Kap123, Kap104 and Pse1.
source: The eS26D33N mutant efficiently binds to Kap123, Kap104 and Pse1 (Figure 6E).
evidence: This is shown in Figure 6E by in vitro binding assay.

claim: The eS26C77W mutant interacted weakly with Kap123, Kap104 and Pse1.
source: In contrast, the eS26C77W mutant interacted weakly with these importins (Figure 6E).
evidence: This is shown in Figure 6E by in vitro binding assay.

claim: Nuclear uptake of GFP-eS26D33N was not affected.
source: In agreement with these interaction studies, nuclear uptake of GFP-eS26D33N was not affected (Figure 6F) and the levels of GFP-eS26D33N were strongly reduced upon Tsr2-depletion (Figure 4—figure supplement 2E).
evidence: This is shown in Figure 6F by microscopy.

claim: A growing yeast cell manufactures approximately 200,000 ribosomes during one generation time.
source: A growing yeast cell manufactures ∼200,000 ribosomes during one generation time (Warner, 1999).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to a review article.

claim: Human Tsr2 can rescue the severe growth defect of the Tsr2-depleted strain.
source: Notably, human Tsr2 can rescue the severe growth defect of the Tsr2-depleted strain (Figure 1—figure supplement 1C), strongly suggesting an evolutionarily conserved role of Tsr2 in 40S assembly.
evidence: This is shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1C by growth assay.

claim: eS26 clamps the 3′-end of mature 18S rRNA precisely at the site where the endonuclease Nob1 cleaves the 20S pre-rRNA.
source: eS26 clamps the 3′-end of mature 18S rRNA (Figure 4—figure supplement 3A, right panel; Rabl et al., 2011), precisely at the site where the endonuclease Nob1 cleaves the 20S pre-rRNA.
evidence: This is supported by a citation to a structural study and shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 3A.

claim: Pre-40S subunits that lack eS26 escape nuclear proofreading and are efficiently transported into the cytoplasm.
source: Pre-40S subunits that lack eS26 escape nuclear proofreading and are efficiently transported into the cytoplasm.
evidence: This is inferred from the observation that eS26-depleted cells do not show nuclear accumulation of pre-40S subunits.

claim: Incompletely assembled pre-40S subunits lacking eS26 recruit the endonuclease Nob1 and form 80S-like particles but fail to process 20S pre-rRNA.
source: These incompletely assembled pre-40S subunits recruit the endonuclease Nob1 (Figure 5A) and form 80S-like particles (Figures 1D and 2C). However, they fail to process 20S pre-rRNA (Figures 1C and 2B), an essential pre-requisite to form a mature 40S subunit.
evidence: This is supported by data shown in multiple figures.

claim: The cytoplasmic 20S pre-rRNA cleavage functions as one of the checkpoints that prevent incompletely assembled, pre-40S subunits from entering translation.
source: We propose that the cytoplasmic 20S pre-rRNA cleavage functions as one of the checkpoints that prevent incompletely assembled, pre-40S subunits from entering translation.
evidence: This is a proposed model based on the data.

claim: RanGTP is unable to efficiently release uL14 (human Rpl23a) from importin 7 (RanBP7).
source: Intriguingly, like in the case of Kap123:eS26 complex, RanGTP is unable to efficiently release uL14 (human Rpl23a) from importin 7 (RanBP7) (Jäkel and Görlich, 1998).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to a previous study.

claim: Yeast r-proteins (uS14, eS31a and eS8a) bound to Kap123 were not released upon RanGTP treatment.
source: Moreover, we found that yeast r-proteins (uS14, eS31a and eS8a) bound to Kap123 were not released upon RanGTP treatment (Figure 4—figure supplement 4) suggesting that these r-proteins may require specific escortins for their release.
evidence: This is shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 4 by in vitro dissociation assays.

claim: Affinity purifications coupled to mass spectrometry have identified more than 200 non-ribosomal factors that are directly involved in ribosome assembly.
source: Affinity purifications coupled to mass spectrometry have identified >200 non-ribosomal factors that are directly involved in ribosome assembly (Bassler et al., 2001; Harnpicharnchai et al., 2001; Dragon et al., 2002; Fatica et al., 2002; Grandi et al., 2002; Nissan et al., 2002; Schäfer et al., 2003).
evidence: This is supported by citations to multiple proteomic studies.

claim: Aggregating r-proteins in the nucleolus aggravate the toxicity of a Caenorhabditis elegans Huntington disease model and decrease their lifespan.
source: Aggregating r-proteins in the nucleolus aggravate the toxicity of a Caenorhabditis elegans Huntington disease model and decrease their lifespan David et al. (2010), emphasizing the importance to safely transfer r-proteins to the assembling pre-ribosomes.
evidence: This is supported by a citation to a study on protein aggregation.

claim: Tsr2 is required for cytoplasmic processing of 20S pre-rRNA to mature 18S rRNA.
source: Tsr2 is required for cytoplasmic processing of 20S pre-rRNA to mature 18S rRNA
evidence: This is the title of a results section and is supported by multiple experiments.

claim: eS26 is recruited to the earliest pre-ribosomal particle, the 90S.
source: eS26 is recruited to the earliest pre-ribosomal particle, the 90S
evidence: This is the title of a results section and is supported by TAP purifications and microscopy.

claim: eS26 is imported primarily by Kap123 and Kap104 into the nucleus.
source: eS26 is imported primarily by Kap123 and Kap104 into the nucleus
evidence: This is the title of a results section and is supported by in vitro binding assays and microscopy.

claim: Kap123 targets Tsr2 to the nucleus.
source: Kap123 targets Tsr2 to the nucleus
evidence: This is the title of a results section and is supported by microscopy of importin mutants.

claim: Tsr2 dissociates importin:eS26 complexes in a RanGTP-independent manner.
source: Tsr2 dissociates importin:eS26 complexes in a RanGTP-independent manner
evidence: This is the title of a results section and is supported by in vitro dissociation assays.

claim: Tsr2 shields eS26 from proteolysis and aggregation, and promotes a safe transfer to the 90S pre-ribosome.
source: Tsr2 shields eS26 from proteolysis and aggregation, and promotes a safe transfer to the 90S pre-ribosome
evidence: This is the title of a results section and is supported by proteolysis assays, aggregation assays, and TAP purifications.

claim: An eS26 mutant associated with Klippel-Feil syndrome in Diamond-Blackfan anemia patients is impaired in importin binding.
source: An eS26 mutant associated with Klippel-Feil syndrome in Diamond-Blackfan anemia patients is impaired in importin binding
evidence: This is the title of a results section and is supported by in vitro binding assays.

claim: Newly synthesized eS26 is transported from the cytoplasm into the nucleus by importins.
